sentences.text: The holotype specimen — the specific fossil used to define the species — is a partial skeleton including a skull found in the Aptian-aged Twin Mountains Formation.
This individual was a subadult when it died.
Researchers estimated the subadult to be between 2.5 and 3 meters long.
Because the holotype was not fully grown, the adult size of Convolosaurus remains unknown.
A unique trait of Convolosaurus is that the premaxilla bears four teeth with a vertical trough on the outside.
The neck vertebrae are opisthocoelous, meaning they are convex at the front and concave at the rear.
The name Convolosaurus means "flocking lizard" because fossils were found in a dense concentration at Proctor Lake in Texas, a density that gave the genus its name from the Latin word for "to flock."

Fossils from the site have been combined into three mounted skeletons displayed at the Proctor Lake US Army Corps of Engineers Office, the Perot Museum of Nature and Science, and the Fort Worth Museum of Science and History.
James "Rusty" Branch discovered the fossil site in May 1985, noting it was one of the richest Lower Cretaceous sites in North America.
The discovery of the site was reported in the scientific literature in 1988.
The species Convolosaurus marri was formally named and described in 2019 by Kate A. Andrzejewski, Dale A. Winkler, and Louis Leo Jacobs.
Only one fossil occurrence of Convolosaurus has been recorded so far.
Convolosaurus lived during the Early Cretaceous period, specifically the Aptian age.
Convolosaurus is classified as a basal ornithopod dinosaur, positioned between Hypsilophodon and Thescelosaurus in the evolutionary tree.
The placement of Convolosaurus reversed previous views because it shares two supraorbitals with Thescelosaurus, suggesting Hypsilophodon lost this trait independently.
Convolosaurus belongs to the family Tenontosauridae.
Convolosaurus is classified within the dinosaur class Ornithischia.
